Decolors can help us understand unfamiliar date formats and [numeral systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_numeral_systems#Standard_positional_numeral_systems). Equivalent [b10]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} and [b54]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base54"} [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} have the same Decolor. To assign a Decolor to a [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}, we need the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. When the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} is unknown and cannot be obtained, it is best to forgo Decolor labeling entirely, as in @tbl-woy above, instead of randomly choosing 1 of the 7 possible Decolors. # Day of month (dom) {#sec-dom} Dec year+day dates can be expanded to display the "beginning of month" ([bom](#bom){#beginningofmonth .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}) and "[International Organization for Standardization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization#:~:text=an%20independent%2C%20non%2Dgovernmental%2C%20international%20standard%20development%20organization)" ([ISO](#iso){#internationalorganizationforstandardization .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"}) [dom]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}. We can think of the [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} as [Dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} 0 even though no such [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} exists. The [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} is the day before the first [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} because [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} are one-based. To obtain a [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}, we can subtract a [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} from a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}: \${monthNumberColor} = \${dotyInputColor7} − \${dayofmonthColor()}. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| label: boundsliders1 //| class: sliders //| code-copy: false Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 364 + leapInput], {step: 1, label: "Day of year"}), viewof dotyInput) Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([-365 - leapInput, -1], {step: 1, label: "Day of year"}), viewof dotyInput1) ``` ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15} $$\text{bom} = \text{pid} - \text{dom}$$ {#eq-bom} ::: We can find every possible [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} by counting index☝️and ring💍fingers as 30 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and other fingers as 31 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, as shown by the hands🤲depicted below. For positive [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, we start counting from -1, which is the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} that precedes the first "month of year" ([moy](#moy){#monthofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"}): [Moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} [0]{.color0}. To cover 12 months with only 10 fingers, the first and last finger each represent 2 months. :::{.hand} ![](/asset/left.svg){.lefthand} ![](/asset/right.svg){.righthand} ::: [[Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Typing-colour_for-finger-positions.svg)]{.handlabel} Like the [knuckle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knuckle_mnemonic#:~:text=a%20mnemonic%20device%20for%20remembering%20the%20number%20of%20days%20in%20the%20months%20of%20the%20Julian%20and%20Gregorian%20calendars)👊and [musical keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Month#:~:text=this%20cyclical%20pattern%20of%20month%20lengths%20matches%20the%20musical%20keyboard%20alternation%20of%20wide%20white%20keys%20(31%20days)%20and%20narrow%20black%20keys%20(30%20days))🎹[mnemonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic#:~:text=any%20learning%20technique%20that%20aids%20information%20retention%20or%20retrieval%20in%20the%20human%20memory), the finger🖐counting technique described above is an attempt to make sense of the irregular pattern of [month lengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Month#:~:text=Name-,Number,of%20days) in the Gregorian calendar. We do not need mnemonics, [rhymes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Days_Hath_September), tables, [dactylonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finger-counting#:~:text=counting%20using%20the%20fingers), or [mental calculations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_calculation#:~:text=arithmetical%20calculations%20made%20by%20the%20mind%2C%20within%20the%20brain%2C%20with%20no%20help%20from%20any%20supplies) to use [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"} or [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"}, because all of the required information is plainly visible in the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}. To convert a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} to or from an [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} month and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, we can use parts of the [`civil_from_days`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#civil_from_days){.mono .under} and [`days_from_civil`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#days_from_civil){.mono .under} algorithms [@hinnant2021date]. [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} months are one-based and [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} are zero-based. [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} Month 1 is [Moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} [10]{.color306by365} and [Moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} [0]{.color0} is [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} Month 3. We can obtain a [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} by plugging a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into @eq-pid2moy or an [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} month into @eq-month2moy. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16} $$\text{moy} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{pid} \ast 5 + 2}{153}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-pid2moy} $$\text{moy} = (\text{isomonth} + 9) \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 12$$ {#eq-month2moy} $$\text{isomonth} = (\text{moy} + 2) \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\bmod} 12 + 1$$ {#eq-moy2month} $$\text{bom} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{moy} \ast 153 + 2}{5}\right\rfloor - \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{UTC offset} \ge 0\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}$$ {#eq-moy2bom} $$\text{dom} = \text{pid} - \text{bom}$$ {#eq-dom} ::: [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} months and [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} are shifted in relation to each other because the Dec epoch, [0000]{.color0}+[000]{.color0}, occurred 2 months or 60 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} after the start of [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} [Year 0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Years:~:text=1%20BC%20is%20labelled%20%2B0000): [-0001]{.color99by100}+[306]{.color306by365}. To convert between [yoe]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="years of era"} and "[common era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era#:~:text=conventions%20used%20in%20the%20Gregorian%20or%20Julian%20calendar%20to%20specify%20whether%20the%20year%20is%20before%20or%20after%20the%20epoch) years" ([cey](#cey){#commonerayear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"}), we add 1 to the [yoe]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} or subtract 1 from the [cey](#cey){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"} if the [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} is greater than [305]{.color305by365}, the [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of year"} is greater than [9]{.color275by365}, or the [ISO](#iso){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International Organization for Standardization"} month is less than [3]{.color0}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17} $$ \text{cey}=\text{yoe}+\begin{cases} 1&{\begin{aligned} &\text{ if } \text{pid} \ \ \ \ \gt 305\\ &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{moy}\ \ \ \gt 9\\ &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}\text{isomonth}\lt 3\end{aligned}}\\\\ 0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases} $$ {#eq-cey} ::: A similar adjustment is needed when dealing with negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets. Dec does not permit "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) to be negative and therefore adds one day to every negative [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}. @eq-moy2bom takes into account the possibility of a negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset and adjusts the [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} accordingly. Starting from zero, we can count every adjusted [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} on our fingers. :::{.hand} ![](/asset/leftnegtzo.svg){.lefthand} ![](/asset/rightnegtzo.svg){.righthand} ::: [[Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Typing-colour_for-finger-positions.svg)]{.handlabel} The adjusted [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} pictured above are identical to the values in the rightmost column of the first table under the heading "[Computing day-of-year from month and day-of-month](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html#Computing%20day-of-year%20from%20month%20and%20day-of-month)" in [[`chrono`]{.mono .under}-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html) [@hinnant2021date]. If [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} were zero-based rather than one-based, we would add one to the right-hand side of @eq-moy2bom. According to @eq-moy2bom, a [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} should expand to ⌊([moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"}×153+2)÷5⌋, but in Dec dates we can interchange [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} and [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} as if they were equivalent: [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} = ~~⌊(~~[moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"}~~×153+2)÷5⌋~~. By prepending zeros until it reaches a set number of digits for [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"}: 3, [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"}: 3, [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}: 2, [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"}: 2, and [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"}: 2, Dec helps us discern between various expanded date types. ## Object Oriented Programming {#oop} Dec dates can be described in the context of [object oriented programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming#:~:text=a%20programming%20paradigm%20based%20on%20objects). In this analogy, a [class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_(programming)#:~:text=a%20syntactic%20entity%20structure%20used%20to%20create%20objects) is a blueprint for Dec dates and an [object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instance_(computer_science)#:~:text=a%20specific%20occurrence%20of%20a%20software%20element%20that%20is%20based%20on%20a%20type%20definition) represents a specific Dec date. When we create an object, we can specify the date that it will represent by providing either a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} for it to store or a [cey](#cey){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"}, month, and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} for it to transform into a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"}. Regardless of the input, only a [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} are stored as [instance variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instance_variable#:~:text=each%20instantiated%20object%20of%20the%20class%20has%20a%20separate%20copy). Our class must define one [instance method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_%28computer_programming%29#:~:text=a%20procedure%20associated%20with%20an%20object) for every potential output that is not an instance variable. Instance methods can use instance variables to produce their output. For example, a method based on Equations -@eq-pid2moy, -@eq-moy2month, -@eq-moy2bom, and -@eq-dom could turn a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into a month and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}. @fig-conv below visualizes how an object that represents the UNIX epoch would convert its [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} and [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} into a [cey](#cey){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="common era year"}, month, [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}. For simplicity, @fig-conv omits the [coe](#coe){.under .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="cycle of era"}, [yoc](#yoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of cycle"}, and [doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"} needed to convert a Dec date into a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"}, the [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} and [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} required to split a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} into a month and a [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, and the negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset adjustment for [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}. ::: {#fig-conv .doxdiagram} ::: # Misaligned unit difference (mud) {#sec-mud} Unlike weeks, Gregorian calendar months differ in length and therefore are not amenable to Dec date expansion. With a constant number of "days in month" ([dim]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days in month"}), we could expand [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"} into [dim]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days in month"}×[moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"}. If [dim]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days in month"} were a multiple of 7 and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} reset at the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}, we could use a "week of month" ([wom](#wom){#weekofmonth .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of month"}) to expand [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"} into [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}+[wom](#wom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of month"}×7 or [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} into [wom](#wom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of month"}×7+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}. With a [dim]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days in month"} of 28, months would align with weeks and would be very close to aligning with a year: 364 = 13 × 28. A [dim]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days in month"} of 35 would align months with both weeks and [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}: 35 = 7 × 5. Sadly, the Gregorian calendar avoids all aligned alternatives, slams shut the perennial paradise pearly gates, and condemns its users to [Sisyphean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisyphus#:~:text=tasks%20that%20are%20laborious%2C%20futile%2C%20and%20never%2Dending%20are%20therefore%20often%20described%20as%20Sisyphean) struggle against misalignment. Dec confronts measurement unit misalignment with "misaligned unit differences" ([mud](#mud){#misalignedunitdifference .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit differences"}). Instead of redefining misaligned units to bring them into alignment, we can express the [onsets](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/onset#:~:text=A%20setting%20about%3B-,a%20beginning,-.%20synonyms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) of all of the units as a [mud](#mud){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit difference"}, then find the onset of any unit by adding the [counts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_data#:~:text=data%20which%20can%20take%20only%20the%20counting%20numbers%2C%20non%2Dnegative%20integer%20values%20%7B0%2C%201%2C%202%2C%203%2C%20...%7D%2C%20and%20where%20these%20integers%20arise%20from%20counting%20rather%20than%20ranking) of all of the other units to the [mud](#mud){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit difference"}, or obtain a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} by summing the [mud](#mud){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit difference"} with all of the counts. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18} $$ \begin{aligned} \text{mud} &= \text{pid} - \text{dom} - \text{dow} \\ &= \text{bom} - \text{dow} \\ &= \text{bow} - \text{dom} \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-mud} ::: In Decalendar, a count is the number of days that have passed since an onset. @tbl-unit gives examples of count and onset pairs. We do not see the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of year"} in Dec dates because it is always zero. Ignoring [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, there are 12 possible [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"}. There are 372 rather than 54 possible [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"}, because weeks are misaligned with not only months but also years. ::: {#tbl-unit .overflowtable} | Unit | Onset | Count | | ----- | ----- | ----- | | Year | [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of year"} | [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} | | Month | [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} | [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} | | Week | [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} | [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} | ::: Dec date expansion has only one rule, namely that each expanded date should always [simplify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplification#:~:text=the%20process%20of%20replacing%20a%20mathematical%20expression%20by%20an%20equivalent%20one%20that%20is%20simpler) to its equivalent year+day date. As shown in @fig-mud below, [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}, [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"}+[dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}, and [mud](#mud){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit difference"}+[dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}+[dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} all simplify to [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} in compliance with the date expansion rule. In contrast, [woy](#woy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="week of year"} and [moy](#moy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of year"} dates are expected to exclude Even though a month is about as long as a [lunation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#Synodic_month:~:text=the%20average%20period%20of%20the%20Moon%27s%20orbit%20with%20respect%20to%20the%20line%20joining%20the%20Sun%20and%20Earth) and a week is almost as long as one of the four major [lunar phases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_phase#:~:text=the%20new%20moon%2C%20the%20first%20quarter%2C%20the%20full%20moon%2C%20and%20the%20last%20quarter), Gregorian calendar months and weeks are misaligned with the lunar cycle and therefore cannot estimate [moonlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight#:~:text=light%20from%20the%20surface%20of%20the%20Moon%2C%20consisting%20mostly%20of%20reflected%20sunlight%2C%20and%20some%20earthlight) levels. # Day of bimester (dob) {#sec-dob} We can get a sense of how much of the surface of the Moon🌙is illuminated by expanding a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into a "beginning of bimester" ([bob](#bob){#beginningofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"}) and "day of bimester" ([dob](#dob){#dayofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}) instead of a [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of month"} and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, a [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"} and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}, or a [mud](#mud){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit difference"}, [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"}, and [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"}. A Dec common bimester is 59 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} long, which is roughly a tenth of a percent shorter than two lunations: 59.0612 = 2 × [29.5306](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_calendar#cite_note-ESAA-2:~:text=synodic%20month%20as-,29.53059%20days,-or%2029%20days). To obtain a [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}, Dec employs an algorithm based on the [`from_days`](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date/blob/7875f43aa9288d176191c83e8284d61acdd5ab7c/include/date/islamic.h#L2252) [method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_%28computer_programming%29#:~:text=a%20procedure%20associated%20with%20an%20object) of the `year_month_day` [class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_%28programming%29#:~:text=a%20syntactic%20entity%20structure%20used%20to%20create%20objects) in the [`islamic.h`](https://howardhinnant.github.io/date/islamic) [library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_%28computing%29#:~:text=a%20collection%20of%20resources%20that%20can%20be%20used%20during%20software%20development) created by [Howard Hinnant](https://howardhinnant.github.io) -@hinnant2021date. Equations -@eq-dot, -@eq-yot, -@eq-leapcount, -@eq-lunarpid, and -@eq-dob below produce a "day of [tricennium](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tricennium#:~:text=A%20period%20of%20thirty%20years)" ([dot](#dot){#dayoftricennium .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of tricennium"}), a "year of tricennium" ([yot](#yot){#yearoftricennium .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of tricennium"}), and the lunar year version of a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} along the way to transforming a [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of era"} into a [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup20} $$ \text{dot} = (\text{doe} + 8) \bmod 10631 $$ {#eq-dot} $$ \text{yot} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{30\ast\text{dot}+15}{10631}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-yot} $$ \text{leapcount} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{11\ast\text{yot} + 14}{30}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-leapcount} $$ \text{lunarpid} = \text{dot} - 354 \ast \text{yot} - \text{leapcount} $$ {#eq-lunarpid} $$ \text{dob} = \text{lunarpid} - 59 \ast \left\lfloor\dfrac{5\ast\text{lunarpid} + 5}{296}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-dob} ::: :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Julia ::: {.cell} ```{.julia .cell-code} function dob(doe) dot = mod(doe + 8, 10631) yot = (30 * dot + 15) ÷ 10631 lunarpid = dot - 354 * yot - (11 * yot + 14) ÷ 30 return lunarpid - 59 * ((5 * lunarpid + 5) ÷ 296) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` dob (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ```{.julia .cell-code} dob(719468) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 53 ``` ::: ::: ### Observable JavaScript ```{ojs} function dob(doe) { const dot = (doe + 8) % 10631; Given that a common bimester is slightly shorter than 2 lunations, lunar phases and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} slowly drift apart over the 2 or 3 lunar years in between lunar leap days ([Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"} [59]{.color59by60}). Nevertheless, we should typically observe a new🌑moon on [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [0]{.color0} and [30]{.color30by59}, first quarter🌓moon on [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [7]{.color07by59} and [37]{.color37by59}, full🌕moon on [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [14]{.color14by59} and [44]{.color44by59}, and last quarter🌗moon on [Dob]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} [22]{.color22by59} and [52]{.color52by59}. A leap bimester is composed of [Dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"} [0]{.color0} to [59]{.color59by60} and can be split into 2 lunar long months: 2 × 30 = 60. To be fair, we would also see wild variation in the lunation pattern if the "Solar" layout used [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"} instead of [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"} and [x](#x){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} instead of Gregorian calendar months. All solar calendar units are entirely out of step with the lunar phases. Dec dates in the year+[bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"}+[dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} format allow us to track the lunar phases and then sum the [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} to identify dates using [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}, identify seasons using [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of one hundred days"}, gauge progress through the seasons using [doh](#doh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of hectoday"}, or classify days as work or rest days using [dox](#dox){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of xún"}. Just as we can split a solar common year into 73 [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}, we can also divide a bimester into 12 "pentadays of bimester" ([pob](#pob){#pentadayofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays of bimester"}). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup21} $$\text{pob} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{dob}}{5}\right\rfloor$$ {#eq-pob} ::: In general, the moon goes from new moon to waxing crescent in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [0]{.color0} and [6]{.color30by59}, from waxing crescent to waxing gibbous in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [1]{.color05by59} and [7]{.color35by59}, from waxing gibbous to full moon in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [2]{.color10by59} and [8]{.color40by59}, from full moon to waning gibbous in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [3]{.color15by59} and [9]{.color45by59}, from waning gibbous to waning crescent in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [4]{.color20by59} and [10]{.color50by59}, and finally from waning crescent to new moon in [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [5]{.color25by59} and [11]{.color55by59}. The first quarter moon occurs around the middle of [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [1]{.color05by59} and [7]{.color35by59}, while the last quarter moon appears near the center of [Pob](#pob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentaday of bimester"} [4]{.color20by59} and [10]{.color50by59}. Solar common years, lunar leap years, lunar long months, and [x]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="groups of ten days"} can be divided evenly into [p](#p){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentadays"}. Solar leap years, lunar common years, lunar short months, and common bimesters are all only 1 day off from being evenly divisible by 5. Dec lunar years and months are based on the [Lunar Hijri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar#:~:text=a%20lunar%20calendar%20consisting%20of%2012%20lunar%20months%20in%20a%20year%20of%20354%20or%20355%20days) calendar. Whereas Lunar Hijri calendar dates consist of lunar years, months, and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}, the analogous Dec dates comprise solar years, [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of bimester"}, and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"}. It is easier to an calculate the [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"} for a solar year, which is called a "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), than the [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"} of a lunar year, which is called a "lunar year length" ([lyl](#lyl){#lunaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"}). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup22} $$ \text{lunarleap} = \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}(11 \ast \text{yot} + 14) \bmod 30 \ge 19\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-lunarleap} $$\text{lyl} = 354 + \text{lunarleap}$$ {#eq-leap2lyl} $$ \text{lyl} = \text{lunarpid} - \text{lunarnid} $$ {#eq-lunardif} ::: Instead of Equations -@eq-lunarleap and -@eq-leap2lyl, we can obtain the [lyl](#lyl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"} by plugging the lunar [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} and [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} into @eq-lunardif, which is similar to @eq-nid. We can also use lunar [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer days of year"} to find zero-based indexes for bimesters via @eq-bimester or for lunar months via @eq-lunarmonth below. Unlike lunar [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} and [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} pairs, bimester and lunar month indexes cannot be used to obtain [lyl](#lyl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year lengths"}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup23} $$ \text{bimester} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{5\ast\text{lunarpid} + 5}{296}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-bimester} $$ \text{lunarmonth} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{11\ast\text{lunarpid} + 5}{325}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-lunarmonth} $$ \text{bimester} = \left\lfloor\dfrac{\text{lunarmonth}}{2}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-month2bimester} $$ \text{lunarmonth} = 2\ast\text{bimester} + \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{dob} \ge 30\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-bimester2month} ::: Lunar Month 11, the second lunar month of Bimester 5 and the final lunar month of the lunar year, has 30 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} in lunar leap years and 29 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} in lunar common years, whereas any other lunar month has 30 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} if its index is even or 29 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} if its index is odd. The lunar [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} of the first day of Lunar Month 11 is 325. The length of Lunar Month 11 is 325 less than the [lyl](#lyl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"}. Unlike lunar months, bimesters maintain a constant length for 2 × 354 − 59 = 649 or 3 × 354 − 59 = 1003 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. To indicate when the bimester length will change, Dec provides "lunar intercalation differences" ([lid](#lid){#lunarintercalationdifference .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation differences"}), which are like lunar [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer days of year"} that reset after the end of a lunar leap year rather than after any lunar year. In lunar leap years, [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation differences"} and lunar [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer days of year"} are equal. In between lunar leap years, [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation differences"} range from -1063 or -709 to -356. In lunar leap years, [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation differences"} and lunar [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer days of year"} range from -355 to -1. Bimester length changes from 59 to 60 when the [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation difference"} reaches -60. We can use Equations -@eq-dot, -@eq-yot, -@eq-leapcount, and -@eq-lid to turn [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"} into [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation difference"}. A [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation difference"} date consists of a [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation difference"} preceded by the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} of the day after a lunar leap day: \${decDob59yColor}+\${decDob59dColor}−\${decLidColor}. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup24} $$ \text{lid} = \text{dot} - \text{leapcount} - 354\ast\left\lfloor\dfrac{30\ast\text{leapcount} + 15}{11}\right\rfloor - 355 $$ {#eq-lid} $$ \text{lyl} = 355 - \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{lid} < -355\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-lid2lyl} ::: Tracking lunar phases is a great example of how Dec date expansion allows Decalendar to do things that the Gregorian calendar cannot. Even without Dec date expansion, Decalendar is objectively better than the Gregorian calendar in every way, but what really sets Decalendar apart from other calendars is the seemingly limitless flexibility of Dec date expansion. # Moon {#moon} "The sky is the limit" is an understatement, because Decalendar can be adapted for people living on the Moon and other celestial bodies. Rather than days, lunar inhabitants would be best served by "spin orbit intervals" ([soi](#soi){#spinorbitinterval .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"}), which are the inverse of the difference in the [sidereal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidereal#:~:text=Sidereal%2C%20meaning%20%22-,of%20the%20stars,-%22%2C%20may%20refer%20to) frequencies of a [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_rotation#:~:text=the%20rotation%20of%20planet%20Earth%20around%20its%20own%20axis) of the Earth on its axis and an [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_of_the_Moon#:~:text=the%20Sun.%20It-,orbits%20Earth,-in%20the%20prograde) of the Moon around the Earth. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup25} $$ \dfrac{1}{1\div\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#:~:text=4.09%20seconds%28%2C%20or-,0.99726968,-of%20a%20solar}{0.99726968}-1\div\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#:~:text=stars%20%28Latin:%20sidera%29:-,27.321661,-days%20%2827%20d%29}{27.321661}} = 1.03505011 $$ {#eq-soi} ::: The number of [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} per mean [tropical year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_year#:~:text=the%20time%20that%20the%20Sun%20takes%20to%20return%20to%20the%20same%20position%20in%20the%20sky) is [365.2421897](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_year#:~:text=1%2C%202000%2C%20was-,365.2421897,-or%20365%C2%A0ephemeris) ÷ 1.03505011 = 352.87391999. We can match this quite closely by setting the lunar Decalendar (Decalunar) [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} to 352 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} if the year is evenly divisible by 8 and to 353 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} otherwise: 7 ÷ 8 − 0.87391999 = 0.00108001 ≈ 1 ÷ 926. For greater precision, the Decalunar [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} could be calculated as in @eq-lunarsyl. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup26} $$ 353 - \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{y} \bmod 8 = 0 \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor} \text{y} \bmod 926 = 463 \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-lunarsyl} ::: The Decalunar epoch should be a new moon that occurs close to midnight on [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day"}[0]{.color0} so that the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and the "[soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"} of year" ([soy](#soy){#soiofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of year"}) would have a common origin and therefore be easier to compare. The initial Decalunar epoch is the [boy](#boy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"} of [1976]{.color76by100}, the year of the [last lunar probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_lunar_probes#:~:text=Lunar%20exploration%20%281959%E2%80%93-,1976,-%29) of the [Space Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race#:~:text=a%2020th%2Dcentury%20competition%20between%20the%20Cold%20War%20rivals%2C%20the%20United%20States%20and%20the%20Soviet%20Union%2C%20to%20achieve%20superior%20spaceflight%20capability), but a later epoch should be chosen once the Moon is permanently inhabited. In Decalunar, a lunar leap year is 343 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} instead of 355 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, a lunar common year is 342 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} rather than 354 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, a bimester is 57 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} in lieu of 59 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, a short month is 28 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} as opposed to 29 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, and a long month is 29 [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"} instead of 30 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. Decalunar monitors lunations by expanding a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into a [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and "[soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"} of bimester" ([sob](#sob){#soiofbimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of bimester"}) rather than a [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"}. A Decalunar lunar common year can be split evenly into 6 bimesters or 3 [quadrimesters](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/quadrimester#:~:text=A%20period%20of%20four%20months%20or%20about%20four%20months): 342 = 6 × 57 = 3 × 114. Decalendar and Decalunar can follow the same lunar leap year pattern because the fractional part of 12 [synodic months](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#Synodic_month:~:text=the%20average%20period%20of%20the%20Moon%27s%20orbit%20with%20respect%20to%20the%20line%20joining%20the%20Sun%20and%20Earth) is nearly identical for days and [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit intervals"}: [29.53059](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_month#Synodic_month:~:text=synodic%20month%29%20is-,29.53059%20days,-or%2029%20d) × 12 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 ≈ 354.367 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 ≈ 354.367 ÷ 1.03505 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1 ≈ 342.367 [mod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder) 1. Decalunar relies on the same [syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"} as Decalendar for precise timekeeping over long periods, and therefore can adapt whenever the [lyl](#lyl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar year length"} diverges from observed lunations. If needed, we can move a day or two between the [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of bimester"} or a [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"} or two between the [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"} and [sob](#sob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of bimester"} to better match lunar observations without affecting the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} or [soy](#soy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="soi of year"} as per Equations -@eq-sob and -@eq-bobplusdob. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup27} $$ \text{soy} = \text{bob}_{\text{s}} + \text{sob} $$ {#eq-sob} $$ \text{doy} = \text{bob}_{\text{d}} + \text{dob} $$ {#eq-bobplusdob} ::: # Mars {#mars} Serendipitously, Earth and Mars rotate on their respective axes almost at the same rate. A Martian [sol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_sol#:~:text=for%20sun%29%20is-,a%20solar%20day%20on%20Mars,-%3B%20that%20is%2C%20a) is [1.02749125](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_sol#:~:text=1.02749125%20Earth%20days) [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, which is about 0.76% of a day less than a [soi](#soi){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="spin orbit interval"}. The Martian variant of Decalendar is called Dec[arean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_adjectivals_and_demonyms_of_astronomical_bodies#Planets:~:text=Martian%2C%20Martial%2C-,Arean,-%5B9%5D) after [Ares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares#:~:text=Greek%20god%20of%20war%20and%20courage), one of the twelve Olympians and the god of war in Greek mythology. Decarean leap years are determined by cycles of 22 years or 14709 sols. In a Decarean cycle, there are 9 short years with 668 sols and 13 long years with 669 sols. Years that are not evenly divisible by 2 always have 669 sols, which is easy to remember because odd years have an odd number of sols. There are also 2 even years with 669 sols every cycle which are always 10 years apart within a cycle and 12 years apart between cycles. The Decarean epoch is 1953+084.41516515, matches the currently used system for [numbering Martian years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Year_numbering:~:text=beginning%20May%2024%2C%201953), has the same fractional part as the [Mars Sol Date epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Mars_Sol_Date:~:text=a%20running%20count%20of%20sols%20since%2029%20December%201873), and coincides with the Martian [northward equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Definition_of_year_and_seasons:~:text=0-,northward%20equinox,-1%2C%202%2C%203), but is otherwise [arbitrary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timekeeping_on_Mars#Year_numbering:~:text=the%20choice%20as-,%22arbitrary%22,-%2C%20the%20great%20dust). I first designed Decarean with [Martian colonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_Mars#:~:text=establishing%20permanent%20human%20settlements%20on%20the%20planet%20Mars) in mind, but now I believe humanity should concentrate on [robotic spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight#Uncrewed:~:text=without%20people%20on%20board). As our technology improves, the cost of sending robots into space will decrease and the return on investments into robotic missions will increase. In contrast, [human spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight#:~:text=spaceflight%20with%20a%20crew%20or%20passengers%20aboard%20a%20spacecraft) will remain expensive and limited by human anatomy and physiology. More importantly, robots are much less likely than astronauts to [contaminate Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interplanetary_contamination#:~:text=It%20is%20thought%20that%20many,may%20have%20already%20been%20contaminated.) with biological material from Earth. We need to avoid contamination so as not to complicate the search for [extraterrestrial life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterrestrial_life#:~:text=life%20that%20originates%20from%20another%20world%20rather%20than%20on%20Earth) or traces thereof on Mars. Natural resources should only be collected from Martian sites that can be confirmed to never have harbored extraterrestrial life. We should first focus exclusively on exploration, then can begin exploitation, but should refrain from colonization of Mars. # Venus {#venus} Even if we can prove without a doubt that Mars is and always has been devoid of extraterrestrial life, we still should not invest resources into enabling Mars to support human inhabitants, because those resources are much better spent on [terraforming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraforming_of_Venus#:~:text=transform%20Venus%20from%20a%20planet%20hostile%20to%20life%20to%20one%20that%20could%20sustainably%20host%20humans) and then [colonizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization_of_Venus#:~:text=establishing%20human%20settlements%20on%20the%20planet%20Venus) Venus, the planet that is [most similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus#:~:text=similar%20to%20Earth%20in%20size%20and%20mass%20and%20is%20often%20described%20as%20Earth%27s%20%22sister%22%20or%20%22twin%22) to Earth in size, mass, composition, and orbit. Whereas Venus should be the focal point for colonization, the Moon and its L1 and L2 [Lagrange points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_point#:~:text=points%20of%20equilibrium%20for%20small%2Dmass%20objects%20under%20the%20gravitational%20influence%20of%20two%20massive%20orbiting%20bodies) will form the central hub for spaceflight. The proximity of the Moon allows for efficient communication with Earth. At light speed, radio signals can travel from Earth to the Moon in 1.24 to 1.41 Dec seconds ([s](#s){#second .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}), Venus in 132 to 907 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, or Mars in 190 to 1390 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}. To put these numbers in context, the speed of light is around 7.195 [taur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_(angle)#Tau_proposals:~:text=%E2%81%A0%20turn-,Circumference%20of%20a%20circle,-%F0%9D%90%B6) ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) per [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, the [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is about 1 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}, there are exactly 90000 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or 86400 [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units#:~:text=the%20world%27s%20most%20widely%20used%20system%20of%20measurement) ([SI](#si){#internationalsystemofunits .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="International System of Units"}) seconds in 1 day, and the approximate distance from Earth ranges from 9 to 10 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} for the Moon, 950 to 6525 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} for Venus, 1365 to 10000 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} for Mars, and 14700 to 24200 [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} for Jupiter. Mars lies near the outer edge of the [habitable zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitable_zone#:~:text=the%20range%20of%20orbits%20around%20a%20star%20within%20which%20a%20planetary%20surface%20could%20potentially%20support%20liquid%20water) and is the outermost [terrestrial planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet#:~:text=a%20class%20of%20planet%20that%20is%20composed%20primarily%20of%20silicate%2C%20rocks%2C%20or%20metals) in our [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System#:~:text=the%20gravitationally%20bound%20system%20of%20the%20Sun%20and%20the%20masses%20that%20orbit%20it). The nearest possibly habitable [exoplanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet#:~:text=a%20planet%20outside%20the%20Solar%20System), [Proxima Centauri b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxima_Centauri_b#:~:text=an%20exoplanet%20orbiting%20within%20the%20habitable%20zone%20of%20the%20red%20dwarf%20star%20Proxima%20Centauri%20in%20the%20constellation%20Centaurus), is roughly 1 billion (10^9^) [c](#c){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"} away. The pool of nearby [potentially habitable exoplanets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_potentially_habitable_exoplanets#Main_list:~:text=a%20list%20of%20confirmed%20exoplanets%20within%20the%20circumstellar%20habitable%20zone%20that%20are%20either%20under%2010%20Earth%20masses%20or%20smaller%20than%202.5%20Earth%20radii%20and%20thus%20have%20a%20chance%20of%20being%20rocky) may expand in the future, perhaps due to the [Big Crunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Crunch#:~:text=the%20expansion%20of%20the%20universe%20eventually%20reverses%20and%20the%20universe%20recollapses) or a [galaxy merger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_merger#:~:text=when%20two%20%28or%20more%29%20galaxies%20collide) involving the [Milky Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milky_Way#:~:text=the%20galaxy%20that%20includes%20the%20Solar%20System). While we study potentially habitable exoplanets, we can create a habitable planet in our own backyard by terraforming Venus. To speed up the process, many terraformation approaches can be pursued in parallel. [Flybys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flyby_(spaceflight)#:~:text=a%20spaceflight%20operation%20in%20which%20a%20spacecraft%20passes%20near%20another%20body) of asteroids or comets could increase the [rotational speed of Venus and expand its orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraforming_of_Venus#cite_note-45:~:text=move%20a%20planet%20in%20its%20orbit%2C%20or%20increase%20the%20speed%20of%20rotation) to bring it into the habitable zone and closer to Earth. An expanded orbit would cool Venus and a faster rotational speed might promote the development of a protective [magnetosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetosphere#:~:text=a%20region%20of%20space%20surrounding%20an%20astronomical%20object%2C%20such%20as%20a%20planet%20or%20other%20object%2C%20in%20which%20charged%20particles%20are%20affected%20by%20that%20object%27s%20magnetic%20field). Venus has an [axial tilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axial_tilt#:~:text=the%20angle%20between%20an%20object%27s%20rotational%20axis%20and%20its%20orbital%20axis) that is just [7.3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus#:~:text=the%20axial%20tilt-,177.36%C2%B0,-.) [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} short of a half turn and therefore has no seasons. Without the need to monitor seasonal changes on Venus, the [Venusian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_adjectivals_and_demonyms_of_astronomical_bodies#Planets:~:text=%5B7%5D-,Venusian,-%2C%20Cytherean) Decalendar (De[cyther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_adjectivals_and_demonyms_of_astronomical_bodies#Planets:~:text=Venusian%2C-,Cytherean,-cythero%2D)) can focus on tracking Venusian solar days. On Venus, a solar year is 224.7 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and a solar day is 116.75 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}. A Decyther cycle lasts 467 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} and can be split into 4 quadrimesters that are 116.75 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} on average: 467 ÷ 4 = 116.75. Each Decyther quadrimester can be divided into 2 bimesters named after the two halves of a day on Earth: [ante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12-hour_clock#:~:text=%2C%20translating%20to%20%22-,before%20midday,-%22%29%20and%20p.m) and [post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12-hour_clock#:~:text=%2C%20translating%20to%20%22-,after%20midday,-%22%29.%5B1). Antes always last 58 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}, but posts can be 58 or 59 [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"} long. Each Decyther cycle comprises four antes and four posts. Any ante or the third post in every Decyther cycle can be evenly split into two Venusian short months: 58 ÷ 2 = 29. The other three posts consist of a Venusian short month and a Venusian long month: 59 = 29 + 30. Decalendar and Decyther have the same epoch and both derive their units from [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"}. Equations -@eq-venusdoc to -@eq-venusdom below turn [doe](#doe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of era"} into Decyther [doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of cycle"}, "days of quadrimester" ([doq](#doq){#dayofquadrimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of quadrimester"}), [dob](#dob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of bimester"}, and [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"}. To track Venusian solar days, Decyther expands the Decalendar [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} into a "beginning of quadrimester" ([boq](#boq){#beginningofquadrimester .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of quadrimester"}) and [doq](#doq){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of quadrimester"} as shown in @eq-venusboq. The [boq](#boq){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of quadrimester"} is the Venusian equivalent of midnight on Earth, the start of [Doq](#doq){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of quadrimester"} 0, and the boundary between quadrimesters. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup28} $$ \text{doc}_♀ = \text{doe} \bmod 467 $$ {#eq-venusdoc} $$ \text{doq}_♀ = (\text{doc}_♀ + \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{doc}_♀ \ge 350\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]}) \bmod 117 $$ {#eq-doq} $$ \text{dob}_♀ = \text{doq}_♀ - 58 \ast \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{doq}_♀ \ge 58\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-venusdob} $$ \text{dom}_♀ = \text{dob}_♀ - 29 \ast \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{dob}_♀ \ge 29\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-venusdom} $$ \text{pid} = \text{boq}_♀ + \text{doq}_♀ $$ {#eq-venusboq} ::: Similarly, the beginning of [Doq](#doq){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of quadrimester"} 58 is the Venusian equivalent of noon on Earth and separates an ante from the post that follows it. Apart from its North and South poles, the surface of Venus receives sunlight during the second half of an ante and the first half of a post ([daytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20the%20day%20in%20which%20the%20Sun%20is%20above%20the%20local%20horizon%20in%20a%20given%20location)), but not during the second half of a post and the first half of an ante ([nighttime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20darkness%20when%20the%20Sun%20is%20below%20the%20horizon)). Regardless of whether we start the zero-based indexing of bimesters from the [boe](#boe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of era"}, the "beginning of cycle" ([boc](#boc){#beginningofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of cycle"}), or [boq](#boq){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of quadrimester"}, a Decyther bimester is an ante if its index is even or a post if its index is odd. Equations -@eq-qoc to -@eq-moc below transform Decyther [doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of cycle"} into "quadrimesters of cycle" ([qoc](#qoc){#quadrimesterofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadrimesters of cycle"}), cycle-based bimester indexes, and "months of cycle" ([moc](#moc){#monthofcycle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="months of cycle"}). ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup29} $$ \text{qoc}_♀ = \left\lfloor\dfrac{4\ast\text{doc}_♀ + 1}{467}\right\rfloor $$ {#eq-qoc} $$ \text{bimester}_♀ = 2\ast\text{qoc}_♀ + \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{doq}_♀ \ge 58\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-venusbimester} $$ \text{moc}_♀ = 2\ast\text{bimester}_♀ + \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{[}\text{dob}_♀ \ge 29\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise}{]} $$ {#eq-moc} ::: [Qoc](#qoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadrimester of cycle"} 2 is one day shorter than the other three [qoc](#qoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadrimesters of cycle"}, because its post, Bimester 5, is one day shorter than the other three posts in a cycle. The missing day is called an extracalation and can be attributed to [Moc](#moc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of cycle"} 11, the second month of Bimester 5. Instead of indexes, Decyther tells us when a day will go missing using "Venusian extracalation differences" ([ved](#ved){#venusianextracalationdifference .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Venusian extracalation differences"}). In Decyther, [ved](#ved){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Venusian extracalation differences"} count down the days until the end of [Doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"} 349, the final day of [Qoc](#qoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadrimester of cycle"} 2, Bimester 5, and [Moc](#moc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of cycle"} 11. Therefore, [ved](#ved){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Venusian extracalation differences"} are the Decyther analog of Decalendar [lid](#lid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lunar intercalation differences"}. Equations -@eq-ved2doc and -@eq-doc2ved below convert between [ved](#ved){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Venusian extracalation differences"} and Decyther [doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of cycle"}. To produce a [ved](#ved){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Venusian extracalation difference"} date, we append a [ved](#ved){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Venusian extracalation difference"} to the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} of Decyther [Doc](#doc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of cycle"} 350, the first day of [Qoc](#qoc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quadrimester of cycle"} 3, Bimester 6, and [Moc](#moc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="month of cycle"} 12. ::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup30} $$ \text{doc}_♀ = (\text{ved} + 817) \bmod 467 $$ {#eq-ved2doc} $$ \text{ved} = (\text{doc}_♀ + 117) \bmod 467 - 467 $$ {#eq-doc2ved} ::: Venus and Mars often appear to be dissimilar to Earth in completely opposite ways and it seems that when one is similar to Earth, the other is not. For example, the axial tilts of Earth, Mars, and Venus are 6.51, 7.00, and 49.27 [centiturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredths of a turn"}, respectively. The unique characteristics of these three planets present an opportunity to showcase the versatility of Decalendar. # Summary {.unnumbered #tldr} At its heart❤️, Decalendar is a simple system that measures time solely in integer years and days. A Dec [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} date is essentially an abbreviation of [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}+[pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}/[syl](#syl){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}, which is a math expression that sums the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} with the fraction of the year that has elapsed. The difference between the denominator and the numerator of this fraction is the number of days left in the year. Dec can expand a date to display different kinds of information without changing the decimal year value that the date represents. Date expansion allows Decalendar to use measurement units other than years and days, such as bimesters, months, and weeks. The simplest expanded dates show an onset, such as a [bob](#bob){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of bimester"}, [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"}, or [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of week"}, and the number of days since that onset. By expanding year+day dates into [bow](#bow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of week"}, [bom](#bom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginnings of month"}, and [mud](#mud){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="misaligned unit differences"} dates, Decalendar provides better support for monthly and weekly schedules than even the Gregorian calendar. Thanks to date expansion, Decalendar can be adapted to work on planets as different as Venus, Earth, and Mars. Therefore, Decalendar can be referred to as ***the*** calendar or the one calendar [to rule them all](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Ring#:~:text=One%20ring%20to%20rule%20them%20all)! # Next {.unnumbered #next} After reading this article, you should be able to understand my motivation for customizing [Quarto](/quarto) and the examples in my [filter](/quarto/filter) and [include](/quarto/include) articles.
